newsitem.title: USA: Christian conservatives take credit in Congress vote.
newsitem.headline: Christian conservatives take credit in Congress vote.

text.p: Christian conservatives claimed credit on Wednesday for keeping Republicans in control of Congress, which analysts said may be more in line with the religious right's controversial agenda than the group that took over Conmgress in 1994.

The Christian Coalition, which distributed 45 million voter guides in the last days of the campaign, boasted a record turnout for a presidential election. According to the group's figures, more than one in four voters nationwide was a self-described born-again Christian.

"For the first time in 68 years a Republican Congress has been re-elected, and it would never have happened without conservative people of faith who provided the margin of victory," said Ralph Reed, executive director of the coalition, which claims 1.8 million members.
"Conservative evangelicals were the firewall that prevented a Bob Dole defeat from mushrooming into a meltdown all the way down the ballot."

Despite Dole's loss to President Bill Clinton, the Republican Party increased its 53-47 Senate majority by at least one. But the party's 235-197 majority in the House of Representatives was expected to shrink by at least nine seats.
Political analysts say the results in both chambers pointed to a new "southernization" of the Republican majority on Capitol Hill.
As a result, the House and Senate next year will have more Republican lawmakers tied to the Protestant fundamentalist electorate of the South's so-called Bible Belt.
"Candidates with ties to the Christian Right did quite well," said James Guth, a political scientist at Furman University in Greenville, South Carolina.

"Many of these people are themselves members of conservative Protestant faiths and traditions -- Southern Baptists, Assembly of God people -- who were not well represented before 1994. They are even more numerous now."

The Republican Party's two new U.S. senators in the South -- Alabama Attorney General John Sessions and Arkansas Republican Tim Hutchinson -- both defeated their Democratic rivals after making strong appeals to Christian conservative voters on social issues, including abortion.

Experts also point out that while Republicans lost 16 House seats in the more moderate North, preliminary results showed them gaining new conservative members in Alabama, Arkansas, Mississippi and Texas.

"Southern Republicans are more conservative than Northern Republicans. Southern Republicans are substantially more conservative than Southern Democrats. And the Southern Republican runs reasonably well with Christian conservatives," said University of Georgia professor Charles Bullock.

In 1994, when Republicans captured both houses of Congress for the first time in 40 years, religious activists hoped the new conservative ethic would mean progress on a social agenda that included a constitutional amendment to allow prayer in schools and the elimination of the Department of Education.
But those proposals went nowhere. Instead, Christian voters had to be content with a federal law allowing states to deny recognition of same-sex marriages.
"Now, the situation in Congress is a little improved for Christian conservatives," said Guth.
